summary: מֶלֶךְ is a king, and מָלַךְ is to be or become king; the nouns name kingship, royal dignity, a reign, or the kingdom ruled, and scripture applies them both to human rulers and to Yahweh’s rule. King and reign stand in the same consonants in Ugaritic, Phoenician, Moabite, Sabaic, Ge’ez, Arabic, Akkadian and Aramaic. The spelling also holds counsel: Aramaic מְלֵךְ “counsel” (Dan 4:24), perhaps Neh 5:7, and the Peshitta’s verbs for advising and promising, as Akkadian and Aramaic use the root for advising and deciding. No verse joins the two meanings, and the cognates cannot separate them.

senses.definition: The ruler of a people or territory.

evidence.note: Four rulers are each named as king of a place.
Zion’s king comes to her, righteous and lowly, riding on a donkey; quoted of Jesus in Mat 21:5 and Jhn 12:15.

senses.definition: God named as the one ruling his people and the earth.

evidence.note: God is king of all the earth.
“I am Yahweh … the creator of Israel, your king.”

evidence.locator: Psa.2.2, מַלְכֵי → βασιλεῖς; Zec.9.9, מַלְכֵּךְ → βασιλεύς σου

senses.definition: Hold or begin to hold kingship over a people.

evidence.note: The kings of Edom reigned before a king reigned over Israel.

senses.definition: Exercise kingship, said of Yahweh.

evidence.note: Yahweh will reign for ever and ever.
Yahweh reigns, clothed in majesty.
In asking for a king the people have rejected Yahweh from reigning over them.

senses.definition: Cause someone to occupy the royal office.

evidence.note: Shechem’s leaders make Abimelech king.
The king makes Esther queen in Vashti’s place.
Yahweh regrets that he made Saul king.

senses.definition: Be placed in kingship by another; this stem occurs once.

evidence.note: Darius was made king over the kingdom of the Chaldeans.

senses.gloss: consider inwardly; be moved to a decision
senses.definition: Nehemiah’s heart acts upon him before he challenges the nobles. “I took counsel with myself” (or “my heart decided for me”) and “my heart ruled over me” are two readings of the construction. The counsel reading has Aramaic מְלֵךְ “counsel” (Dan 4:24), Aramaic מְלַךְ “decide, advise” and Akkadian “his heart counsels him” beside it; the single occurrence does not settle it.

evidence.note: וַיִּמָּלֵךְ לִבִּי עָלַי precedes Nehemiah’s rebuke of lending at interest.

senses.definition: The territory and people under a king.

evidence.note: Babel and other cities form the beginning of Nimrod’s kingdom.
Israel is to be to Yahweh a kingdom of priests, a holy nation: a people ruled by him.
Peter applies Exo 19:6 to believers.
Yahweh alone is God of all the kingdoms of the earth.

senses.definition: Kingship as authority exercised or transferred.

evidence.note: The kingdom is torn from Saul’s hand and given to David.

senses.definition: Before another noun, belonging to the king: the royal city, the royal family, the royal house.

evidence.note: David asks why he should live in the royal city with Achish.
Gibeon is like one of the royal cities.
Athaliah destroys all the royal seed.
Bethel is the king’s sanctuary and a royal house.

senses.definition: Royal standing and authority, also characterizing a royal crown or garment.

evidence.note: A crown of royalty is placed on Esther’s head.

senses.definition: The rule a king exercises, the realm under that rule, or its duration.

evidence.note: God’s kingdom and dominion endure through all generations.
Four kingdoms arise from the nation.

senses.definition: A royal woman, whether a reigning queen or a king’s queen.

evidence.note: The queen of Sheba comes to test Solomon.
Esther acts as queen in reporting the plot.

senses.definition: The office or authority of a king, and royal status.

evidence.note: Samuel sets out the judgment or rule of the kingship.
The kingship is Yahweh’s, and he rules over the nations.

senses.definition: In “seed of royalty”, the royal family or lineage.

evidence.note: Ishmael is of royal descent.

senses.definition: A royal realm or the period of its ruler; a less frequent formation beside מַמְלָכָה.

evidence.note: The kingdom of Og names his territory.
The beginning of Jehoiakim’s reign dates the prophecy.

senses.definition: The title of the deity to whom cakes, incense, and drink offerings are given in Jeremiah. The title identifies a female recipient; these passages do not give her a personal name.

evidence.note: Cakes are made for the queen of the heavens.
The worshippers make cakes depicting her and pour offerings to her.

senses.definition: A ruler addressed or described by his royal title.

evidence.note: Nebuchadnezzar is called king of kings, whose authority the God of heaven gave him.

senses.definition: A king’s rule or the realm entrusted to him.

evidence.note: Kingdoms arise in succession.

senses.definition: The period during which a king rules.

evidence.note: The temple is finished in the sixth year of Darius’s reign.

senses.definition: The royal woman who comes to the banquet and advises the king.

evidence.note: The queen enters and speaks to the king.

senses.definition: Advice offered to someone; attested once in Biblical Aramaic.

evidence.note: Daniel asks that his counsel please the king and urges righteousness and mercy to the poor.

senses.definition: A ruler holding the royal office.

evidence.note: Herod is called king.

senses.definition: A female royal ruler.

evidence.note: The queen of the south came to hear Solomon’s wisdom.

senses.definition: Royal authority or the realm ruled, including the kingdom of heaven or of God.

evidence.note: The kingdom of heaven has drawn near.

senses.definition: The continuing exercise of kingship.

evidence.note: His reign will have no end.

senses.definition: Offer a course of action.

evidence.note: Caiaphas had advised that one man should die for the people.
“I counsel you to buy from me gold refined by fire.”

senses.definition: Give one’s word that something will be done.

evidence.note: Abraham is assured that God can fulfill what he promised.
God promised Abraham and swore by himself.

senses.definition: Be the object or recipient of a promise.

evidence.note: Promises were made to Abraham and his seed.

senses.definition: Confer together concerning a proposed course.

evidence.note: They take counsel together to seize and kill Jesus.

senses.definition: Exercise royal power.

evidence.note: He will reign over the house of Jacob forever.
“We do not want this man to reign over us.”

words.summary: One Syriac verb counsels, promises and (in the aphel) reigns. Its promising has no cognate of its own: a promise is a course of action declared and bound upon oneself, as counsel is one proposed to another and a decision (Aramaic מְלַךְ “decide”, Akkadian malāku “come to a decision”) one settled. That link is drawn from the shared verb, not shown by a verse.

senses.definition: Advice or a course agreed upon, including a hostile plan.

evidence.note: They take counsel against him, how to destroy him.

senses.definition: An undertaking or assurance given, often what God has promised.

evidence.note: Jesus sends the promise of his Father.

words.summary: The noun of the verb’s promising. Its tie to the root runs through the verb, which also means to counsel; no cognate language has a word for promise from this root.

cognates.note: The expression is “king of kings”; the noun is the comparison for the royal title.

doctrine.statement: Daniel tells the king that the God of heaven gave him his kingdom (Dan 2:37). The vision later gives enduring dominion and kingdom to one like a son of man, and the kingdom to the people of the holy ones (Dan 7:13–14, 27). Luke announces that Jesus will receive David’s throne and reign over Jacob’s house without end (Luk 1:32–33). In these passages kingship is authority God gives, and the kingdom he gives to his son and his people does not pass to another.

Yahweh says he has set his king on Zion (Psa 2:6), and the apostles read the psalm of Jesus, against whom the kings of the earth took their stand (Act 4:25–27). Zechariah tells the daughter of Zion that her king comes to her, righteous, saved and lowly, riding on a donkey (Zec 9:9); Matthew and John say this was done when Jesus rode into Jerusalem (Mat 21:4–5; Jhn 12:14–15). Jeremiah’s branch of David is a king who will reign and act wisely and do justice in the land (Jer 23:5).

At Sinai Yahweh tells Israel that if they obey his voice and keep his covenant they will be to him a kingdom of priests and a holy nation (Exo 19:5–6). Peter gives these words to those who believe in Christ (1Pe 2:9), and in Revelation the redeemed are made kings and priests to God, who will reign on the earth (Rev 1:6; 5:10). The people Yahweh rules is also the people who serve him and will share his rule.

note:
One Hebrew verb holds the reign and counsel uses: m.cd.ae and m.ce.aa match the same occurrences, so only m.cd.ae is assigned. Its support count cannot distinguish those meanings. Neh 5:7 remains explicitly uncertain: the local translation reads “my heart reigned over me”; counsel-language has Aramaic and Akkadian beside it. מְלֶכֶת is a common title, so it is included; מֹלֶךְ, מִלְכֹּם, personal names, and the Malkielite gentilic are left for name entries. The Syriac king/queen lexeme is one SEDRA row, but the feminine word is displayed separately. Malchus (SEDRA 1780) is a proper name. Cognates of counsel are deliberately not assigned to reign, and conversely.

One root or two (2026-11-09, evidence only). No letter of מלכ is a merged letter, so sounds cannot split the senses. (1) King/rule/kingdom: Ugaritic, Phoenician, Moabite, Sabaic, Ge’ez, Arabic, Akkadian (malku, malkatu, malkūtu) and Aramaic. (2) Possess/own: Arabic malaka, Ge’ez malaka, Sabaic hmlk, Phoenician M-L-K II (Krahmalkov p. 285); never in scripture’s Hebrew or Aramaic. (3) Counsel/decide: only Akkadian (malāku A, māliku, milku, malku C), Aramaic (מְלַךְ rule/decide/advise in one verb, Jastrow; Dan 4:24) and Syriac (one verb counsel/promise/reign, Payne Smith p. 277), and in Hebrew perhaps Neh 5:7. Akkadian keeps malku “king” and malku C “counsel, decision” as two headwords (CAD M/1 pp. 166, 169) but spells malku A also maliku, the spelling of māliku “counselor”, and its lists equate maliku with šarru “king”; malku C is “(divine) decision”, bēl malki “decision maker”. So where counsel occurs it sits in the same languages as king, and “decide” is the common ground (the one whose decision stands rules), but no text shows the step from one to the other. CAD notes malāku B “to rule” at Ras Shamra as a West Semitic word (p. 158).

Syriac promise: Payne Smith p. 277 lists the peal as I. counsel, advise; II. promise; III. reign, and the pael likewise. It is linked by kin to the counsel noun מֵלְכָּא, not by a cognate: no cognate language has “promise”. Open question for the user: keep the kin link, or leave promise unlinked and flagged.

Not consulted: CAL (refuses automated access), so no Old/Imperial Aramaic inscriptions are cited; CAD M/2 for milku (Oracc only); Leslau CDG. Fisher 1969 has no mlk pair. Phoenician mmlkt is “person of royal lineage; king” (Krahmalkov p. 293), not “kingdom”: it is named on the construct sense “royal” of מַמְלָכָה and on “royal descent” of מְלוּכָה only.
